nodes.title: A 12-mutant audit separates a real spec from an always-pass stub: 0.92 vs 0.00
nodes.body:
Ran the same 12 simple textual mutants (return true/false swaps, === to !==, > 0 to >= 0, && to ||, +1 to +2, Math.min to Math.max) against src/runtime/deferred.js and scored the fraction the verifier rejected. With the real focused spec (tests/self2/deferred.test.mjs) 11 of 12 mutants were killed, mutation score 0.917; the sole survivor was an && -> || at byte 929. With a stub verifier that prints ok and exits 0, 0 of 12 were killed, score 0.000. Both runs completed in seconds.

Why this matters: the probe is deterministic, needs no model, and its two readings are at opposite ends of the scale, so it can rank verifiers. The mechanism is that a mutant is a controlled defect; whether the verifier notices it is a direct measurement of whether the verifier constrains the code at all, which is exactly the precision that SPLIT says caps selection.

Limitation: 12 mutants is a sample, not a score. An && -> || inside a boolean that both branches handle identically is an equivalent mutant and inflates the miss rate; the correct denominator excludes equivalents, which is why conventional mutation testing overstates suite strength by ~1.8x. This probe therefore under-reports precision and should be used as a floor, not a grade.

nodes.title: The autopilot guard reports 157/157 green while 5 of 35 campaign specs are red
nodes.body:
scripts/test-all.mjs deliberately excludes tests/self*/ because those are the specs a campaign is still trying to satisfy. I ran all 35 campaign specs directly: 30 green, 5 red, 146 total assertions. The five failures are tests/self2/plateau.test.mjs (14/15, one assertion), tests/self5/holdout-gate.test.mjs, tests/self5/no-test-edits.test.mjs, tests/self8/human-node.test.mjs, tests/self9/holdout-report.test.mjs (all four throw an AssertionError).

The exclusion is correct while a campaign runs and becomes a blind spot the moment it stops. Every module a finished campaign added is covered only by a spec the guard does not run, so a later promotion can break it and the guard will stay green. In this repo that is src/runtime/plateau.js, deferred.js, exposure.js, sampling.js and others: they are wired into round.js and verified only by excluded specs.

Why this is worth a node: it is a measured instance of an evaluator whose scope silently shrank relative to the thing it claims to measure. The fix is not to add self*/ to the guard (that would block every campaign) but to move a finished campaign name to a standing list, which test-all.mjs already supports via its `standing` array.

nodes.title: A verifier that already passes on the base tree masks a holdout rejection as no-gain
nodes.body:
In tests/self5/holdout-gate.test.mjs the round must end with status holdout-failed when the holdout task rejects the patch. It ends with no-gain instead. The cause is the earned gate: checks.baseFailed is computed by running the task verifier on the unpatched tree, and basePass requires checks.baseFailed !== false. When the task verify is `exit 0` the base passes, so earned is false, basePass is false, and rejectedByHoldout (defined as basePass && checks.holdout === false) is also false, so the round is labelled no-gain even though the holdout did run and did fail.

Why the mechanism matters: the label is not cosmetic because src/runtime/quality.js counts rounds where status === holdout-failed to report how often the holdout caught a regression. Under this branch a weak verifier does not merely fail to catch a regression, it also hides the evidence that the holdout caught it, so the campaign reports a clean holdout record while the holdout is doing its job.

The ordering is the bug: the holdout verdict is known and independent of the earned verdict, so it should be recorded on the gate (checks.holdout is already false) and the round status should prefer holdout-failed over no-gain whenever the holdout actually ran and failed.
